shortExplanation: The square terms cancel, leaving -300+3.
detailedSteps: Expand the first product to $10000-300$ and the second parenthesis to $10000-3$. Subtracting yields $-300+3=-297$.
keyIdeas: Distributing before subtraction
commonMistakes: Distributing the final minus sign incorrectly.
difficultyNotes: The difference lies in whether the 3 is multiplied by 100.

shortExplanation: The meetings use 135 of the 540 workday minutes.
detailedSteps: The second meeting lasts $2\cdot45=90$ minutes, so the combined time is 135 minutes. The workday is $9\cdot60=540$ minutes.
The percentage is $100(135/540)=25$.
keyIdeas: Meeting time as a fraction of the workday
commonMistakes: Comparing minutes to hours without converting units.
difficultyNotes: Use the same time unit in numerator and denominator.

shortExplanation: Four socks can all differ, but five cannot.
detailedSteps: With four colors, any five socks include two of one color by the pigeonhole principle. Four do not guarantee a pair, because one of each color can be selected.
Both facts show the minimum is 5.
keyIdeas: A matching pair by the pigeonhole principle
commonMistakes: Giving a sufficient bound without checking it is minimal.
difficultyNotes: A worst-case selection establishes necessity.

shortExplanation: The three operation values are 1,3,6.
detailedSteps: The defining formula is $H(x)=(x+x^2)/2$. Hence $H(1)+H(2)+H(3)=(2+6+12)/2=10$.
keyIdeas: The average of a value and its square
commonMistakes: Using x squared alone or averaging the three final inputs together.
difficultyNotes: Evaluate the unary operation separately on each argument.

shortExplanation: Monday and Wednesday must both belong, or both not belong, to the three extra days.
detailedSteps: A 31-day month has four complete weeks plus three consecutive surplus weekdays. Monday and Wednesday appear equally often exactly when both receive a surplus occurrence or neither does.
The possible first weekdays are Monday (surplus Monday-Tuesday-Wednesday), Thursday (Thursday-Friday-Saturday), and Friday (Friday-Saturday-Sunday). There are three.
keyIdeas: Three surplus weekdays in a 31-day month
commonMistakes: Counting only the case when Monday and Wednesday each occur five times.
difficultyNotes: Equality also holds when both weekdays occur only four times.

shortExplanation: The inscribed angle is half the 50-degree central angle.
detailedSteps: Because AB is a diameter and $\angle COB=50^\circ$, A lies outside the minor arc CB. Angle CAB intercepts that arc.
The inscribed-angle theorem gives $\angle CAB=50^\circ/2=25^\circ$.
keyIdeas: An inscribed angle intercepting a central arc
commonMistakes: Using the central angle itself as the inscribed angle.
difficultyNotes: Identify the common intercepted arc.

shortExplanation: The triangle area is 48, so the rectangle length is 12.
detailedSteps: The isosceles triangle altitude is $\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=8$, giving area $12\cdot8/2=48$.
The width-4 rectangle therefore has length $48/4=12$ and perimeter $2(12+4)=32$.
keyIdeas: Equal areas between a triangle and rectangle
commonMistakes: Reporting the area or only the longer rectangle side.
difficultyNotes: The isosceles altitude bisects the base.

shortExplanation: The positive price divides both 48 and 64.
detailedSteps: The ticket price x must be a positive integer divisor of $\gcd(48,64)=16$. Its possible values are $1,2,4,8,16$, a total of five.
keyIdeas: Common divisors as ticket prices
commonMistakes: Including zero as a whole-number ticket price despite positive purchases.
difficultyNotes: Both groups buy integral numbers of tickets.

shortExplanation: Only the signs of c and e change between the two evaluations.
detailedSteps: The correct expression expands to $a-b+c-d-e$. Without parentheses, the written sequence becomes $a-b-c-d+e$.
Equality requires $c-e=-c+e$, hence $e=c=3$.
keyIdeas: A coincidental equality after dropping parentheses
commonMistakes: Changing every sign after each minus without respecting the nesting.
difficultyNotes: Cancel the terms unchanged by the parenthesis error.

shortExplanation: Solve the distance equation in minutes.
detailedSteps: Let t be the rainy minutes, leaving $40-t$ sunny minutes. The speeds are $1/3$ and $1/2$ mile per minute, respectively.
Thus $t/3+(40-t)/2=16$. Multiplying by 6 yields $2t+120-3t=96$, giving $t=24$.
keyIdeas: Travel at two different speeds
commonMistakes: Using hours for speeds but minutes for the time variable.
difficultyNotes: Convert the two rates before forming the linear equation.

shortExplanation: Coupon A is best from 200 through 250 dollars.
detailedSteps: At listed price p, the savings are $0.15p$, 30, and $0.25(p-100)$. Coupon A matches or exceeds B when $p\ge200$.
It matches or exceeds C when $0.15p\ge0.25p-25$, or $p\le250$. Thus $x=200$, $y=250$, and $y-x=50$.
keyIdeas: A discount optimal on a closed price interval
commonMistakes: Applying coupon C to the entire listed price.
difficultyNotes: An optimality region is the intersection of two inequalities.

shortExplanation: The changed fraction ranges from 20 to 80 percent.
detailedSteps: Let p percent change from No to Yes and q percent change from Yes to No. Then $p-q=20$ and $x=p+q=20+2q$.

The final No group has size 30 percent, so $0\le q\le30$. Both endpoints are achievable: only 20 percent switch to Yes at the minimum; all original No students change to Yes, while 30 percent of the class change from original Yes to No at the maximum.
Thus $x_{\min}=20$, $x_{\max}=80$, and their difference is 60.
keyIdeas: Minimum and maximum changed responses
commonMistakes: Assuming every change must be from No to Yes.
difficultyNotes: Net change and total change need not coincide.

shortExplanation: The solutions are 12,20,60.
detailedSteps: The right side is nonnegative, so $x\ge0$. For $0\le x\le15$, the equation is $x=60-4x$, giving $x=12$.
For $15\le x\le30$, it is $x=4x-60$, giving $x=20$. For $x\ge30$, the inner absolute value is $2x-60$, so the right side is the constant 60 and $x=60$.
Each value belongs to its interval and satisfies the original equation. Their sum is $12+20+60=92$.
keyIdeas: Three intervals for a nested absolute value
commonMistakes: Accepting a root of a linear branch that lies outside that branch.
difficultyNotes: Each absolute-value sign change introduces a new interval.

shortExplanation: There are 100 entries, including x.
detailedSteps: The fixed entries sum to $99\cdot100/2=4950$. Therefore $(4950+x)/100=100x$.
It follows that $9999x=4950$, or $x=50/101$.
keyIdeas: An average involving its own unknown
commonMistakes: Dividing by 99 instead of including x as the hundredth entry.
difficultyNotes: The average is 100x, not 100.

shortExplanation: The total attempted count gives an upper bound of 29 correct answers.
detailedSteps: Let c and w be correct and incorrect counts. The score condition is $4c-w=99$, so $w=4c-99$.
Because $c+w\le50$, $5c-99\le50$, giving $c\le29.8$. Thus $c\le29$. The choice $c=29,w=17$ leaves four blanks and realizes the score, so the maximum is 29.
keyIdeas: A score constraint with unattempted questions
commonMistakes: Requiring all 50 questions to have been attempted.
difficultyNotes: Prove that the maximum bound is actually attainable.

shortExplanation: Each cap subtends 60 degrees at the center.
detailedSteps: The circle radius is $r=\sqrt3/3$, larger than the center-to-side distance $1/2$ but smaller than the center-to-corner distance $\sqrt2/2$. Thus four disjoint caps lie outside the square.
A side cuts a cap whose half-angle satisfies $\cos\theta=(1/2)/r=\sqrt3/2$, so $\theta=30^\circ$. The cap area is $\pi r^2/6-\tfrac12r^2\sin60^\circ=\pi/18-\sqrt3/12$.
Multiplying by four gives $2\pi/9-\sqrt3/3$.
keyIdeas: Four equal circular caps outside a square
commonMistakes: Subtracting the entire square area even though its corners lie outside the circle.
difficultyNotes: Check which object contains the side midpoint and which contains the corners.

shortExplanation: The school count lies between 22 and 24 and must be odd, forcing 23.
detailedSteps: If there are s schools, there are $3s$ students. With distinct scores and one median student, $3s$ is odd and Andrea has rank $(3s+1)/2$.
Carla at rank 64 requires $3s\ge64$, so $s\ge22$. Andrea outranks Beth at rank 37, requiring $(3s+1)/2<37$, hence $s\le24$.
Since s is odd, the only possibility is $s=23$. Its median rank is 35, consistent with both teammate ranks.
keyIdeas: A median rank above both teammates
commonMistakes: Placing the median below Beth even though Andrea has the highest team score.
difficultyNotes: Distinct scores make the rank inequalities strict.

shortExplanation: Condition on whether a is divisible by three.
detailedSteps: The interval has 670 numbers of each residue modulo 3. If $a\equiv0$, the expression $a(bc+b+1)$ is divisible by 3 automatically, contributing probability $1/3$.
For nonzero a, require $b(c+1)+1\equiv0$. Among the nine pairs of residues for b,c, the successful pairs are $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$.
keyIdeas: Uniform residues modulo three
commonMistakes: Treating the three summands as independently distributed residues.
difficultyNotes: Factor out a before analyzing the remaining residues.

shortExplanation: Two algebraic side lengths arise, but only 6 places O outside the triangle.
detailedSteps: Let the side be s, put $M=(0,0)$ at the midpoint of BC, and put $A=(0,h)$ with $h=s\sqrt3/2$. The circle center lies on AM extended, with coordinate $y_O=h\pm4\sqrt3$.
The radius condition is $s^2/4+y_O^2=156$. With the plus sign it becomes $s^2+12s-108=0$, whose positive root is 6. With the minus sign it becomes $s^2-12s-108=0$, whose positive root is 18.
For $s=18$, $y_O=5\sqrt3$ lies strictly between 0 and $h=9\sqrt3$, so O is inside the equilateral triangle and is excluded. For $s=6$, O lies beyond A, so the required side is 6.
keyIdeas: Excluding an interior circumcenter placement
commonMistakes: Keeping the side 18 while ignoring the outside-triangle condition.
difficultyNotes: Geometric placement conditions select among algebraic roots.

shortExplanation: The radii are H/3 and 3H, a ratio of nine.
detailedSteps: Extend BC and FA to their intersection V. These lines form a $60^\circ$ wedge. If the perpendicular distance from V to AB is H, regular-hexagon geometry puts DE at distance 3H from V.
Each circle center is on the wedge bisector. A center distance d from V gives radius $d\sin30^\circ=d/2$. For the first circle, external tangency above AB gives $d=H-r$, so $r=(H-r)/2$ and $r=H/3$.
For the second circle below DE, $d=3H+R$, so $R=(3H+R)/2$, giving $R=3H$. Hence $R/r=9$ and the area ratio is 81.
keyIdeas: Circles in a 60-degree wedge
commonMistakes: Using the base-distance ratio three as the radius ratio.
difficultyNotes: The two circles lie on opposite exterior sides of the parallel hexagon edges.

shortExplanation: The middle digit must be 0 or 7.
detailedSteps: A four-digit palindrome has value $1001a+110b$, where $a=1,\ldots,9$ and $b=0,\ldots,9$. Since $1001$ is divisible by 7 and $110\equiv5\pmod7$, divisibility requires $b\equiv0\pmod7$.
Two of the ten middle-digit choices, 0 and 7, work for every a. The probability is $2/10=1/5$.
keyIdeas: A four-digit palindrome modulo seven
commonMistakes: Assuming the remainder is uniform just because the numbers are chosen at random.
difficultyNotes: A decimal place-value formula exposes the divisibility condition.

shortExplanation: Apply inclusion-exclusion to assignments with an empty required bag.
detailedSteps: Every distinct candy has three bag choices, so there are $3^7$ assignments. Those with the red bag empty number $2^7$, and the same is true for the blue bag.
The one assignment putting everything in the white bag was removed twice and must be added back. Thus the count is $3^7-2\cdot2^7+1=1932$.
keyIdeas: Two required nonempty bags
commonMistakes: Treating the white bag as required to be nonempty.
difficultyNotes: Only the two specified bags enter the exclusion conditions.

shortExplanation: Encode entries by their rows and count the permitted prefix states.
detailedSteps: Place 1 through 9 in increasing order, recording only which row receives each next entry. Each row must receive three entries. Column increase holds exactly when every prefix has row counts $a\ge b\ge c$: a lower row cannot have its kth entry until the row above has its kth entry.
Let $D(a,b,c)$ count valid prefixes. Starting with $D(0,0,0)=1$, use $D(a,b,c)=D(a-1,b,c)+D(a,b-1,c)+D(a,b,c-1)$, taking invalid states or negative indices as zero.
The final entry must go in the bottom row, so $D(3,3,3)=D(3,3,2)=42$. Each valid row word uniquely fills its three rows in increasing order.
keyIdeas: Prefix counts for an increasing array
commonMistakes: Counting arbitrary row partitions without enforcing the column condition.
difficultyNotes: A bijection to prefix counts makes the finite recurrence a complete counting proof.

shortExplanation: Only quarterly scores 5,10,20,40 versus 5,14,23,32 satisfy all constraints.
detailedSteps: Write the increasing geometric ratio as $p/q>1$ in lowest terms. Integral quarterly scores then have the form $Kq^3,Kpq^2,Kp^2q,Kp^3$ for a positive integer K. Their total is $K(p+q)(p^2+q^2)\le100$.
This bound permits only $(p,q)=(2,1),(3,1),(4,1),(3,2)$: $p\ge5$ already makes $p^3>100$, and for $q\ge3$ the smallest reduced case $p=4,q=3$ totals 175.
The arithmetic scores start at the same $Kq^3$ and have positive integral difference d, so their total is $4Kq^3+6d$. The one-point margin requires $K[(p+q)(p^2+q^2)-4q^3]-1=6d$.

For (2,1), $K\le6$ and $11K-1$ is divisible by 6 only when $K=5$, yielding $d=9$. For (3,1), the left side is $36K-1$, never divisible by 6. For (4,1) only K=1 is allowed, giving 80; for (3,2) only K=1 is allowed, giving 32. Neither is divisible by 6.
Thus the first-half total is $(5+10)+(5+14)=34$.
keyIdeas: Integral geometric and arithmetic scoring sequences
commonMistakes: Assuming the geometric ratio is an integer without ruling out rational ratios.
difficultyNotes: Integrality and the score cap reduce the ratio to a short complete list.

shortExplanation: Divisibility forces a multiple of 315, and an explicit polynomial attains 315.
detailedSteps: The number a is an integer because $P(1)=a$. Define $F(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x-5)(x-7)$. Repeated division by these monic linear factors shows $P(x)-a=F(x)Q(x)$ with Q having integer coefficients.
At even inputs 2,4,6,8, the F values are $-15,9,-15,105$. Each therefore divides $P(x)-a=-2a$. Their least common multiple is 315, so $315\mid2a$. As 315 is odd, $315\mid a$, giving $a\ge315$.
To attain the bound, take $Q(x)=-8x^3+124x^2-576x+762$ and $P(x)=315+F(x)Q(x)$. Both have integer coefficients. At odd inputs the F factor vanishes, giving P=315.
At even inputs 2,4,6,8, the Q values are $42,-70,42,-6$. Multiplying by the corresponding F values gives -630 in every case, so P=-315. Thus the smallest a is 315.
keyIdeas: An integer-coefficient polynomial with alternating values
commonMistakes: Proving a divisibility lower bound without constructing an integer-coefficient polynomial that attains it.
difficultyNotes: Monic factor division preserves integer coefficients, and a construction completes the minimum proof.
